DESCRIPTION:
The generic fallback validates the hat's payload against its
    declared schema (task 009) exactly as any dedicated `_step_*` method
    would honour its own sentinel/verdict -- a hat that breaks its own
    trivial contract does not get its edge anyway.

    v0.13 task 003 (#92) strengthens this. The OLD claim, pinned here
    before the cutover, was just: `state in ("failed", "aborted")` and
    `"contract violation" in status["reason"]` -- i.e. a SINGLE bad
    payload ended the run outright, with the abort reason literally
    quoting the schema error. That is `deck-phase3g`'s own shape (#92's
    PRD): a broken contract was fatal on the first offence.

    The NEW claim keeps the old one's real content -- the move is still
    refused on every bad payload, the payload never gets its edge while
    it stays wrong -- and adds what the old assertion could not see at
    all: the specific error reached the hat verbatim on the re-ask, the
    ladder ran the FULL `contract_retry_max + 1` attempts before giving up
    on that one work iteration (never fewer, never more), that exhaustion
    did NOT end the run (`self._abort_reason` stays unset, the SAME hat is
    asked completely fresh instead), and the run went on to SUCCEED once
    the hat's next attempt finally validated. That is strictly stronger:
    everything the old assertion proved is still proved (the bad payload
    never took its edge), plus the survival the old assertion could not
    have distinguished from a crash.

    A one-line mutation that reverts the task-003 cutover -- put back
    `errors = contracts.validate_payload(hat, payload)` /
    `self._abort_reason = message` / `return ("tail",)` in place of the
    `enforce_contract` call in `_step_generic_hat` -- makes this test fail
    on its very first new assertion (`state == "succeeded"`): the
    reverted code sets `_abort_reason` on the FIRST bad payload and
    returns `("tail",)` before the hat ever gets a second chance, so the
    run ends `"aborted"` instead, and only ONE `contract.violation` event
    is ever emitted instead of `attempts_per_ladder`.

    dies immediately -- but it has already spawned a background grandchild
    (its own `sleep 30 &`) before that TERM arrives. `kill_tree` walks
    depth-first and signals every descendant it finds strictly BEFORE the
    pid it was called on, so the grandchild is (in this walk order) signalled
    ahead of the TERM-obeying parent -- but only if the walk can still find
    it. With `pgrep` unreachable and `children_of()` reverted to a
    pgrep-only walk, `children_of(cmd_pid)` finds nothing, so `kill_tree`

    but that leaves the grandchild orphaned and still running its own 30s
    sleep, holding this step's stdout pipe open long after the parent -- and
    this script's own report -- have already finished. A TERM-obeying parent
    proves only that this tree's ROOT was reaped, never that the rest of the
    tree was too; this pins the latter with a parent that dies on its own
    the instant it is signalled, so the only thing that can still be left
    running is a grandchild the walk failed to reach.

    signal the engine's own group, not the child, and the SIGINT never
    reaches it. This drives exactly that window with no real timing race:
    `os.getpgid` is made to report the engine's own pgid for the child pid,
    the shape a genuinely pre-`setsid` child has.

    Mutation case (recorded in the commit message): reverting `interrupt()`
    to the unconditional `os.killpg(os.getpgid(pid), SIGINT)` makes this
    test fail -- `killpg` gets called with the engine's own pgid instead of
    `kill` being called on the child's pid, and the assertions below catch
    that directly rather than through a timing-dependent kill outcome.

    ["reopenedTaskIds"] and _discretionary_gate_available(approach)`, so a
    re-rejection on a signature whose ruling had ALREADY spent its one
    re-park paused a SECOND time under the identical `operator_input_
    needed` pauseReason -- and spent the shared discretionary gate doing
    it -- whenever that gate happened to still be unspent. Measured
    against unfixed code, episode 3 below returned `('advance', 'paused',
    'operator_input_needed')` with `discretionaryGateSpent {'1': True}`.
    A.5's own text bounds the re-park itself ("a one-re-park-per-ruling
    refusal on a re-rejection the ruling already addressed", `docs/
    roadmap.md`'s v0.23 block), not one branch's route to it, and the
    ruling decision already PRE-EMPTS this very branch while it is
    unspent (`mechanical_ruled_park_due`, checked at the top of it) -- so
    the same ruling being exhausted has to let this rejection through,
    exactly as cure task cure-01-02-3 already established for the
    reviewer's own `raise_operator_gate` field, the other door into the
    same spent re-park. The gate the second ruled rejection "cannot use"
    is therefore left UNSPENT for a genuinely different rejection later.

    Three episodes, one on-disk run dir, a fresh `LoopSupervisor` each
    time (this file's own multi-episode convention):

    1. the ruling is filed against the cure-reopen rejection's own
       signature, through the product's ONE ruling writer
       (`RunDir.add_ruling`, which resolves the signature from
       `rejectionSignatures[str(approach)]`). The map is seeded directly,
       as `test_a_re_rejection_on_a_ruled_signature_re_parks_once_and_
       does_not_spend` above already does: the only rejection edge that
       RECORDS a signature for these all-curable findings is condition
       2's own pause, and taking it would spend the very gate this edge
       is about -- which is precisely how the pre-fix reading of this
       probe went wrong. Nothing is spent here: no gate, no cure pass,
       no re-park.
    2. the rejection arrives and matches the ruling, whose re-park is
       unspent: `mechanical_ruled_park_due` re-parks it (`rulingReparked
       == [1]`) and, by construction, spends NO gate --
       `discretionaryGateSpent` is still absent.
    3. the SAME rejection recurs with the ruling now exhausted AND the
       reopen gate still unspent -- the named edge. It proceeds to the
       ordinary cure pass (`rejected_curable_pass_available`), never a
       second `operator_input_needed` pause, and the gate it could not
       use is still unspent.

DESCRIPTION:
The other half of "deliberate": when somebody cancels the iteration's
    own task, the boundary must not eat the cancellation and pretend the
    iteration merely failed.

    Task 029 (#182 family, steer 023/021): `hang()` used to suspend on
    `asyncio.sleep(3600)`, but this suite's own autouse `asyncio.sleep`
    patch (conftest.py, "backoff and sleep stubbed by default") makes
    *every* delay resolve in a single extra event-loop tick -- including
    this one. On 3.11, `asyncio.wait_for` wraps the awaited coroutine in a
    separate `Task` (`ensure_future` + `add_done_callback`), one scheduler
    hop slower than 3.12+'s direct `await fut`; that one extra hop was
    enough for the instant-patched sleep to resolve and `hang()` to return
    *before* `task.cancel()` ran, so no CancelledError was ever raised --
    a fixture race, not an engine defect (task 028's diagnosis). `hang()`
    now suspends on an `asyncio.Event` that nothing in this test, this
    module or the patched-`asyncio.sleep` machinery ever sets -- it cannot
    resolve on its own on *any* interpreter, so the worker task is
    provably still suspended when `task.cancel()` fires, deterministically,
    version-independently.

    Task 029, second pass: this node states BOTH halves of the contract it
    is here to pin -- the `CancelledError` propagates out of
    `_run_iteration_once`, *and* no `iteration.end` event is recorded for
    the cancelled iteration. The second assertion used to live only in the
    sibling `test_a_cancellation_mid_iteration_is_not_turned_into_a_fault`,
    so honouring an outside cancellation and not recording it as a finished
    iteration were pinned by two different nodes; a boundary that honoured
    the cancel *and* emitted an end event would have passed this one. It is
    an added assertion, not a loosened one.
NAME: test_a_cancellation_requested_from_outside_is_honoured
